content: Breastfeeding is a critical aspect of infant nutrition, but not all infants are able to feed directly at the breast. Therefore, evaluating methods of milk expression is essential to ensure optimal outcomes for both mothers and infants. This study aimed to assess the acceptability, effectiveness, safety, impact on milk composition, contamination, and costs of various milk expression methods. The review included 41 trials involving 2,293 participants, with data from 22 trials (1,339 participants) analyzed. Most trials focused on mothers of infants in neonatal units (26 trials, 1,547 participants), while others involved mothers of healthy infants at home (14 trials, 730 participants). One trial included mothers of both neonatal and older healthy infants. The studies compared different methods of milk expression, including hand expression, various types of pumps, and specific protocols or adjunct behaviors such as simultaneous versus sequential pumping, pumping frequency, relaxation techniques, breast massage, and breast cleansing protocols. Due to the heterogeneity of participants, interventions, and outcomes, pooling of findings was not feasible for most outcomes. Consequently, a comprehensive summary of findings table could not be produced. Most results were derived from single studies, and the trials were conducted in 14 countries under diverse circumstances between 1982 and 2015. Sixteen of the 30 trials evaluating pumps or products received support from manufacturers, and the risk of bias varied across studies. Primary Outcomes: 1. Maternal Satisfaction and Acceptability: Only one of 17 studies provided data suitable for analysis. In this study, mothers using an electric pump were more likely to feel self-conscious about being seen while expressing milk compared to those using hand expression (mean difference [MD] 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.15 to 1.25; P = 0.01, participants = 68). Mothers using hand expression found the instructions clearer compared to those using an electric pump (MD -0.40, 95% CI -0.75 to -0.05; P = 0.02, participants = 68). Other studies reported varied satisfaction measures, with no clear preference for a specific pump type. However, some relaxation and support interventions were associated with higher satisfaction. 2. Milk Contamination: No clinically significant differences in milk contamination were observed between hand expression and any type of pump (risk ratio [RR] 1.13, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.61; P = 0.51, participants = 28). Comparisons between manual pumps and hand expression (MD 0.20, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.58; P = 0.30, participants = 142), large electric pumps and hand expression (MD 0.10, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.49; P = 0.61, participants = 123), and large electric pumps and manual pumps (MD -0.10, 95% CI -0.46 to 0.26; P = 0.59, participants = 141) also showed no significant differences. 3. Maternal Breast or Nipple Pain and Damage: Pain levels were similar between large electric pumps and hand expression (MD 0.02, 95% CI -0.67 to 0.71; P = 0.96, participants = 68). One study reported sore nipples in 7% of participants using both manual and large electric pumps, with engorgement occurring in 4% of manual pump users and 6% of electric pump users. No nipple damage was reported in the hand-expression group, while one case of nipple damage was noted in both the manual pump and large electric pump groups. 4. Adverse Effects on Infants: One study examined adverse effects on infants, but the results were excluded as not all infants received their mothers' expressed milk. Secondary Outcomes: 1. Quantity of Expressed Milk: Interventions such as relaxation, music, warmth, massage, early initiation of pumping, increased pumping frequency, and appropriate breast shield size increased milk volume in some studies, with clinically significant results in certain cases. Support programs and simultaneous versus sequential pumping did not show significant differences in milk volume. No pump consistently demonstrated a significant increase in milk volume. 2. Nutrient Quality of Milk: Hand expression and large electric pumps yielded higher protein content compared to manual pumps. Hand expression resulted in higher sodium and lower potassium levels compared to large electric or manual pumps. Fat content was higher when breast massage was combined with pumping. No significant differences in energy content were observed between methods. 3. Hormonal Effects: No consistent effects on prolactin levels or oxytocin release were associated with specific pump types or methods. 4. Economic Aspects: Economic outcomes were not reported in the included studies. Authors' Conclusions: The most appropriate method of milk expression may depend on factors such as the time since birth, the purpose of expression, and the individual needs of the mother and infant. Low-cost interventions, including early initiation of milk expression, relaxation, massage, warming the breasts, hand expression, and lower-cost pumps, may be as effective or more effective than large electric pumps for certain outcomes. Variations in nutrient content across methods may be relevant for specific infants. However, small sample sizes, large standard deviations, and the diversity of interventions necessitate caution in generalizing these findings. Further independent research is needed to evaluate hand expression, relaxation techniques, and other non-commercially driven methods.
